contradiction.viewer_thinks: chilies are literally hot, like an ember
contradiction.actually: a molecule tricks the exact nerves that report real heat

beats.narration: This fruit has no flame, no ember, no heat at all. Yet one bite convinces your whole mouth it is burning. How does a plant fake a burn?
beats.claim: chili heat is a chemical illusion: capsaicin triggers pain without real heat
beats.visual_question: why does a cold fruit feel like fire?
beats.visual_answer: a cross-sectioned chili glowing at the placenta, no flame anywhere

beats.narration: The alarm, at least, is real. Your mouth raises it the same way it reacts to scalding coffee: through the body's built-in heat sensor.
beats.claim: capsaicin and real heat trip the same nerve heat sensor
beats.visual_question: what part of the mouth reacts to a chili?
beats.visual_answer: a nerve ending under the tongue raising the same alarm as boiling coffee

beats.narration: The sensor is called TRPV1. It opens above forty-three degrees Celsius. Capsaicin wedges that same gate open at body temperature, with no heat in sight.
beats.claim: TRPV1 opens above 43 degrees Celsius, and capsaicin opens it without heat
beats.visual_question: how can a molecule open a heat gate without heat?
beats.visual_answer: the TRPV1 channel gate held open by a capsaicin molecule at a cool 37 degrees

beats.narration: Wedged open, the channel floods the nerve with ions, and the nerve sends one message upward: burning. But nothing is actually burning, and at the levels we eat, nothing is damaged.
beats.claim: the burn is a false-alarm signal; capsaicin does not burn tissue at food levels
beats.visual_question: what does the open channel do to the nerve?
beats.visual_answer: ions pouring through the open channel, one word climbing the nerve: BURNING

contradiction.viewer_thinks: water puts out a chili burn
contradiction.actually: capsaicin is fat-loving, so water just smears it around

beats.narration: So why does water make it worse? Capsaicin dissolves in fat, not water. A sip only smears the molecule across fresh territory.
beats.claim: capsaicin is fat-soluble, so water spreads it rather than washing it away
beats.visual_question: why does water fail against capsaicin?
beats.visual_answer: a water droplet pushing oily capsaicin droplets outward instead of removing them

beats.narration: Milk tends to work better. Its casein molecules surround capsaicin and carry it off, a wash more than an antidote.
beats.claim: milk casein binds capsaicin and tends to wash it away better than water
beats.visual_question: why does milk calm the burn?
beats.visual_answer: casein clusters capturing capsaicin droplets in a glass of milk

beats.narration: Birds feel none of this: their heat receptor shrugs capsaicin off. The burn is tuned for mammals alone, and one leading explanation says the plant keeps seed-crushers away while birds carry its seeds far.
beats.claim: bird TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin; the burn is thought to filter seed dispersers
beats.visual_question: who is immune to the chili's burn?
beats.visual_answer: a bird eating a red chili unbothered, seeds scattering beneath it
